query: For high-entropy-alloy protective coatings in wear-resistant applications, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs their wear performance and why? Define a controlled change that would distinguish the hypothesis from a baseline, the directional observations expected if it is correct, the range over which it should hold, the prior evidence that supports it, and an observation that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Increasing the content of an oxide‐forming element (in this case, aluminum) in an already high-entropy alloy protective coating will promote the formation of a continuous, coherent alumina-rich tribolayer during sliding contact, which in turn governs and reduces the coating’s wear by limiting adhesive and abrasive damage.
generation.material_initial_state: High-entropy alloy protective coatings having a balanced, equiatomic (or near-equiatomic) composition deposited via conventional methods that result in a relatively uniform microstructure but with only moderate oxide formation during wear.
generation.intervention: Formulate a variant of the baseline coating by enriching its composition with 10–20% more aluminum (while adjusting the relative proportions of the other elements to retain a high configurational entropy) to enhance oxidation behavior at the contact surface.
generation.conditions: Wear tests under controlled sliding conditions at room temperature in ambient atmosphere with moderate applied load and sliding speed, where tribochemical reactions are significant but not extreme enough to induce thermally driven phase transformations.
generation.structural_mediator: The intervention is expected to drive the in situ development of a nanostructured, continuous, alumina-rich tribolayer that is adherent to the underlying coating.
generation.mechanism: During sliding wear, the excess aluminum selectively oxidizes to form a protective alumina (Al2O3) film. This self-adaptive tribolayer acts as a barrier that reduces direct metal-to-metal and abrasive contact, thereby lowering friction and wear rate.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the baseline coating, the Al-enriched coating will exhibit significantly reduced wear rates and lower friction coefficients as verified by quantifiable metrics (e.g., mass loss, wear track depth, and friction force) along with evidence of a more continuous and coherent alumina-rich layer on the worn surface.
generation.baseline: The baseline is provided by the conventional high-entropy alloy coating with standard (balanced) elemental proportions that only form a less coherent or discontinuous tribolayer during wear, leading to higher observed wear rates under identical conditions.
generation.boundary: This effect is expected to hold under moderate contact pressures and sliding speeds in ambient conditions; however, under highly aggressive wear conditions (extremely high loads, speeds, or temperatures), the kinetics of tribolayer formation may differ, potentially limiting the protective effect.
generation.uncertainty: The quantitative degree of improvement in wear performance (e.g., percentage reduction in wear rate) is uncertain and may vary with microstructural nuances and test conditions. Variations in other alloying elements might also influence oxidation behavior and tribolayer integrity.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of coatings: one with the baseline composition and one with a 15% relative increase in aluminum content. Subject both sample sets to identical controlled sliding wear tests under moderate load and speed in ambient atmosphere. Characterize the wear tracks by measuring mass loss, friction coefficients, and by using SEM/EDS and XPS to examine the continuity and composition of the worn surface tribolayers.
measurements: Mass loss or wear track profile measurements to assess wear rate
Surface morphology and chemical state (Al2O3 presence and continuity) via SEM/EDS and XPS
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Al-enriched coatings do not exhibit statistically significant improvements compared to the baseline (i.e., lower wear rate, reduced friction, and a clearly more continuous, alumina-rich tribolayer) under the given test conditions, then the hypothesis is rejected.
